Edit: Fixed.

tar files have permissions and ownership information.
The tar command has flags that controls these.

By default:

- For a regular user, tar will not set the owner, and filter out priviledged bits from the permissions (because the user can't set them). The process umask is respected.
- For root, tar will set the owner, and set all permission bits. The process umask is ignored.

The implementation isn't considering ownership at the moment, and the permission bits get filtered for priviledged bits but the umask gets ignored.

I think we should default to the regular user `tar` behavior.

To be able to opt into the other mode, the API will need to be extended. This doesn't need to happen now if only the default mode should be supported. Though maybe you want to take it into account already, and for example introduce `ExtractOptions` and add `Overwrite` to it instead of making it an argument.

Seeing a strange test failure coming from `DateTime` that is only happening in the CI. I cannot reproduce it locally in any of the failing configs.
I already discussed this with @tarekgh and my next step is to print the value I'm calculating.

Callstack:
```
System.ArgumentOutOfRangeException : Ticks must be between DateTime.MinValue.Ticks and DateTime.MaxValue.Ticks. (Parameter 'ticks')
Stack Trace:
/_/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/DateTime.cs(183,0): at System.DateTime.ThrowTicksOutOfRange()

/_/src/libraries/System.Formats.Tar/src/System/Formats/Tar/TarHeader.Read.cs(151,0): at System.Formats.Tar.TarHeader.ReplaceNormalAttributesWithExtended(IEnumerable`1 extendedAttributes)
/_/src/libraries/System.Formats.Tar/src/System/Formats/Tar/TarReader.cs(328,0): at System.Formats.Tar.TarReader.TryProcessExtendedAttributesHeader(TarHeader firstHeader, Boolean copyData, TarHeader& secondHeader)
/_/src/libraries/System.Formats.Tar/src/System/Formats/Tar/TarReader.cs(267,0): at System.Formats.Tar.TarReader.TryGetNextEntryHeader(TarHeader& header, Boolean copyData)
/_/src/libraries/System.Formats.Tar/src/System/Formats/Tar/TarReader.cs(106,0): at System.Formats.Tar.TarReader.GetNextEntry(Boolean copyData)
/_/src/libraries/System.Formats.Tar/tests/TarReader/TarReader.File.Tests.cs(461,0): at System.Formats.Tar.Tests.TarReader_File_Tests.Read_Archive_File_LongSymbolicLink(TarFormat format, TestTarFormat testFormat)
```

The tar entry I'm using for the failing tests were all created with the Ubuntu `tar` tool, not by this code. So I'm reading the `double` value stored in the entry header, which has the following value:

`atime = 1649971880.002326`

Tarek gave me a formula to convert from `double` to a `DateTimeOffset`. This is the result I get when I run this code locally in my x64 Ubuntu machine:

`long ticks = (long)(secondsSinceUnixEpoch * TimeSpan.TicksPerSecond) + DateTime.UnixEpoch.Ticks;`

Converting the values from the formula, we get:

`(1,649,971,880.002326 * 10,000,000) + 719,162 = 16,499,718,800,742,422`

And this ticks value is what I pass to the constructor:

`DateTimeOffset offset = new DateTimeOffset(ticks, TimeSpan.Zero);`

The exception comes from the `DateTime` constructor that is called in the `DateTimeOffset` constructor:

```cs
public DateTimeOffset(long ticks, TimeSpan offset) : this(ValidateOffset(offset), ValidateDate(new DateTime(ticks), offset))
{
}
```

This is where the exception is thrown:

```cs
public DateTime(long ticks)
{
  if ((ulong)ticks > MaxTicks) ThrowTicksOutOfRange();
  _dateData = (ulong)ticks;
}
```

I manually calculated the value of `MaxTicks` by looking at all the values it comes from:

`MaxTicks = DaysTo10000 * TicksPerDay - 1 = 3652059 * (10 * 1000 * 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24) - 1 = 3652059 * 864,000,000,000 - 1 = 3,155,378,975,999,999,999`

My value of `ticks` is _not_ larger than `MaxTicks`:

```
16,499,718,800,742,422 (ticks)
3,155,378,975,999,999,999 (MaxTicks)
```

Tarek and I found a bug in `double.TryParse`: If we pass a string that contains a number with a dot, the method sometimes fails to parse the dot, creating a super huge number that obviously `DateTimeOffset` cannot process because it's beyond the `MaxTicks` value. I opened an issue: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/68200

Regarding the string to double conversion problem due to culture - I did this:

```
double.TryParse(str, NumberStyles.Any, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out double number)
```

But it didn't seem to have any effect. In fact, not sure why, but the string I'm passing now shows up with an unexpected comma instead of a dot. I'll keep investigating.

issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: APIs to support tar archives
comments:
Thanks, @carlossanlop.

What about async APIs? Do we need an async version of GetNextEntry, as presumably that does IO? What about WriteEntry? ExtractToFile? AddFile? etc. What about IAsyncDisposable? 

For UnixFileMode, how does this relate to anything we might add around chmod? cc: @eerhardt

TarEntry isn't disposable but contains a Stream. Who's responsible for disposing the stream and when, for both reading and writing?

> What about async APIs

ZipArchive doesn't have async APIs as well (although requested for years now PowerShell/PowerShell#1541). Either both get async APIs or none of them, anything else would be inconsistent.

What are the exact use cases?  

"The community has expressed interest in having .NET offer APIs that would allow creation, manipulation and extraction of tar files."

I think it should be good to get that more written out.

> What about async APIs? Do we need an async version of GetNextEntry, as presumably that does IO? What about WriteEntry? ExtractToFile? AddFile? etc. What about IAsyncDisposable?

I need to think about async APIs a bit more. I mainly wanted to make sure the _sync_ ones made sense. But I do couple of questions:

- Would it be acceptable to add async APIs later? What should we worry about now to ensure we don't cause adding async APIs later becomes a breaking change?
- I think reading the header bytes is quite fast, so I assume making the APIs asynchronous would be to make sure that we don't block when reading from, for example, a network stream, which is not exactly passing all the bytes at once. Is this a correct assumption? Are there any other scenarios you envision as requiring asynchronous APIs?

> Would it be acceptable to add async APIs later? What should we worry about now to ensure we don't cause adding async APIs later becomes a breaking change?

Define "later" :smile: We should review any async APIs as part of the design for the types and we should ship them as part of the same release as the rest of the type.  If we want to add them in a separate PR, that's ok.

> I think reading the header bytes is quite fast, so I assume making the APIs asynchronous would be to make sure that we don't block when reading from, for example, a network stream, which is not exactly passing all the bytes at once. Is this a correct assumption? Are there any other scenarios you envision as requiring asynchronous APIs?

Think of it like this.  Find any calls you're making to anything that might do I/O, e.g. any call to Stream.Read/Write, any call to StreamReader.ReadXx or StreamWriter.WriteXx, etc... any public API that can reach any of those calls should be considered for having an async variant.  The goal is a dev using these APIs to read/write TAR files should never have to synchronously block doing I/O.

> Does this sound acceptable?

So to restate:
- If the TarReader creates the Stream, it will ensure it's properly disposed of as part of TarReader.Dispose.
- If the developer creates the Stream, it's the developer's responsibility to ensure it's disposed of, and the TarWriter won't hold on to any references to it, e.g. WriteEntry will do all the I/O involving the supplied stream and won't store it for subsequent use.

If so, I think that sounds ok.

> What are the exact use cases?
> _"The community has expressed interest in having .NET offer APIs that would allow creation, manipulation and extraction of tar files."_
> I think it should be good to get that more written out.

- The PowerShell team has expressed interest in having APIs to handle tar to simplify their cmdlets, and to enable adding new ones. Some examples or tar-related issues and PRs: https://github.com/PowerShell/Microsoft.PowerShell.Archive/issues/149 , https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/issues/2740 , https://github.com/PowerShell/Microsoft.PowerShell.Archive/issues/22
- The author of SharpCompress [would be happy](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/1540#issuecomment-566419457) to base their own implementation on ours, or even stop supporting theirs altogether, if we can make ours work with seekable and non-seekable streams.
- We have identified places in our own code that could benefit from being able to manipulate tar files with APIs and diagnose issues better, instead of capturing errors from the external `tar` tool. One example (we might find more later): [dotnet/sdk/src/Tests/HelixTasks/TarGzFileCreateFromDirectory.cs](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/a30e465a2e2ea4e2550f319a2dc088daaafe5649/src/Tests/HelixTasks/TarGzFileCreateFromDirectory.cs)

> well, if the user needs to add a tar entry with the contents of a stream, it basically means they want to add a regular file entry.

This is false.
In one of my current work projects, I'm writing an archive (zip, and streaming out to gcloud, but not otherwise relevant) with images that were encoded and output to memory (via [`cv2.imencode(...)`](https://docs.opencv.org/4.5.5/d4/da8/group__imgcodecs.html#ga461f9ac09887e47797a54567df3b8b63)), completely removing the need to touch the filesystem.
I would imagine there are any number of streaming-output scenarios for the web that will work the same.

Ah, that's what you were referring to.
Yes, I assumed that you could use an in-memory stream that way, I was just asking whether we should add a convenience method to streamline that (not need to manually create `entry`, in your example).

@Clockwork-Muse The trouble, as I understand it, is that from "just a stream" there's not enough information to set the uid/gid/LMT/modebits/etc file entry attributes.  Presumably some sort of defaults will apply when going the manual create-from-a-stream approach, but at least there it has the chance of being a bit more in-your-face that it's something you might want to set.

For the async APIs: My understanding, which I'm always clear that I defer to @stephentoub here, is that unless you're @stephentoub and you wrote down the non-generic ValueTask you meant instead non-generic Task.

The only generic one (GetNextEntryAsync) probably stands a chance of not yielding every now and then, so being `ValueTask<T>` might be reasonable.

Next steps:

1. Update the top API proposal with the extra async APIs.
2. Add any necessary corrections related to what Jeremy mentioned above regarding `ValueTask` vs `Task`.
3. Mark this as ready for review.
4. Schedule a meeting with Immo to discuss this proposal.

@stephentoub would you mind giving us your input on no. 2? And any other feedback is also welcome, if you have any.
I mostly agree with Jeremy's take.  GetNextEntryAsync should return `ValueTask<TarEntry?>`, and DisposeAsync has to return `ValueTask`.  Everything else returning Task seems reasonable.

Looking at this API, it seems to me that it tries to precisely model the supported tar formats. But I feel like this precision comes at the cost of convenience and simplicity: it requires the user to understand the details of the formats, when the API could hide these to some extent.

Some examples:

* If I want to write a series of `Stream`s to an archive (as in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/65951#issuecomment-1058415922), I usually don't want to understand which of the formats to use, let alone having to specify it in two different ways. The API should choose a default and use that, unless explicitly specified.
* If I want to read format-specific data, like `ExtendedAttributes`, I don't necessarily want to special case the format that supports it, I just want to understand whether an entry does have the data or not.
* Names of properties should be fully spelled-out (e.g. `ModifiedTime` instead of `MTime`, `UserName` instead of `UName`), to make it easier to understand what they mean.

Adjusting the API this way would make it worse for those who care about the minutia of the tar formats, but I think that's an acceptable tradeoff, to make it easier for the common use.

Another option:

The mtime, atime and ctime fields that are stored directly in the header (not in extended attributes) have a limit of 12 bytes, and are stored as octal integers in ASCII. The maximum number we can store in such location is `777,777,777,777` in octal, or `68,719,476,735` in decimal.

Actually, no: The `mtime` field has to end with a space character, according to the spec (_although... the `tar` tool stores them with a null char at the end instead of a space_). So we only have 11 bytes available for the number. That means the max number in octal is `77,777,777,777` or `8,589,934,591` in decimal. I'll adjust this.

I think the upper bound will cause trouble in V7, Ustar and Gnu, but not in PAX: The advantage of PAX having extended attributes is that we can store values with no length limit. One of the rules is that if we find out that mtime is too large to fit in 12 bytes, we save it as an extended attribute with its full value, and in the header field we only write what fits. Then, when the user needs to consult the `ModificationTime` property, we need to return the correct value we retrieved from the extended attribute, not from the header.

> I'm not sure whether we have the ability to add CA1305

Turning on CA1305 for the repo and doing `build clr.corelib+libs -rc release -warnaserror 0` produces 6,429 warnings (and that's one configuration only). I sanity-checked a few, and all that I looked at were false positives.

> do we have the ability to enable CA1305 just for this library?

Yes, if you _really_ want to, you can create a `.editorconfig` file in the src directory for the library and put this in it:
```
[*.cs]

# CA1305: Specify IFormatProvider
dotnet_diagnostic.CA1305.severity = warning
```

What kind of false positives -- they were formatting for display? The rule AFAIK flags when we do not pass a format provider, so (I think) that can be universally applied - it might simply be redundant in some cases.

If the analyzer flagged a case that is meant for display, then the call-site should pass in `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`/`.CurrentUICulture`. The analyzer doesn't care *what* format provider you pass in, just that you're explicit about what you want, even if that's matching the otherwise implicit behavior.

> then the call-site should pass in CultureInfo.CurrentCulture/.CurrentUICulture

That adds unnecessary expense.  For example, if you call Int32.ToString() and the value is non-negative, it will never have to access CultureInfo.CurrentInfo; if the call site always passes in CurrentCulture, you're now paying for that access regardless.

It also adds unnecessary verbosity... that's 6,429 places extra verbiage is required.

> What kind of false positives

Formatting for display, passed in a case where it won't actually be used, etc.

It also has tons of false negatives, e.g. it won't flag places ToString() is used implicitly, such as in string interpolation, as part of string concatenation, and so on.

> it might simply be redundant in some cases.

In every case I looked at.

> // If the permissions weren't set at all
